title: Hayashi Rice
subtitle: hashed beef and onion in rich tomato sauce over rice
excerpt: Hayashi rice is a Japanese yoshoku dish of thinly sliced beef and onion simmered in a rich, slightly sweet tomato and demi-glace style sauce, served over short-grain rice. It is deeply savoury and satisfying. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Hayashi rice is a Western-influenced Japanese dish from the Meiji era, thought to be a Japanese adaptation of hashed beef, with the flavour profile adjusted for Japanese tastes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the sauce without rice for up to 2 months. Defrost overnight and reheat gently, adding a splash of water if it thickens too much.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. The sauce improves overnight in the fridge.

glossaryTerms.definition: In Japanese home cooking, a rich sauce base made from beef stock, tomato, soy sauce, and mirin that approximates the depth of a classical French demi-glace without the long reduction.
A pre-made Japanese hayashi sauce block, similar to curry roux, that contains the seasoning and thickening for hayashi rice. Sold in Japanese supermarkets.

content.text: depth from slowly caramelised onion, soy sauce, and a
block. The result is a silky, dark sauce with sweet, tangy, and savoury notes. Serves 4.
Taking the time to caramelise the onions properly is the most important step in the recipe. Dark golden onions build the sweetness and depth that defines hayashi rice.
Heat oil and butter in a Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the onions and cook, stirring every few minutes, for 15 to 20 minutes until deep golden and soft. Do not rush this step.
Push the onions to the side. Increase heat to high. Add the beef slices and sear for 2 minutes until browned. Add the mushrooms and cook for 2 more minutes.
Add soy sauce, mirin, and sake. Stir to deglaze the pan. Pour in 600 ml of water and bring to a simmer.
Break the hayashi roux block into pieces and stir into the simmering liquid until fully dissolved. Simmer on low heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is thick and glossy.
Cook the rice in a medium saucepan. Serve the hayashi sauce over a mound of rice in each bowl.

attrs.cause: Not enough roux was used or the sauce was not simmered long enough.
attrs.fix: Simmer uncovered for an extra 5 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.

attrs.cause: The tomato element in the roux was not balanced by enough sweetness.
attrs.fix: Stir in a teaspoon of mirin or a pinch of sugar to balance the acidity.

attrs.cause: The beef slices were too thick or overcooked in the sauce.
attrs.fix: Slice as thinly as possible and only add beef to the sauce for the final 5 minutes of simmering.

content.text: Hayashi rice is one of Japan's best yoshoku dishes. It came from hashed beef but Japan made it sweeter, silkier, and more savoury. The origin of the name is disputed. Some say it came from the English word 'hash', others from a restaurant owner called Hayashi. Either way, it has been served in Japanese homes since the Meiji era and shows no signs of going anywhere.
